standard_prerequisites.use: It gives the alternative route: the Chern roots of $E^\vee$ are the negatives of those of $E$, which produces the same three signs.

core_obligations: Run the first argument: reduce to the case where $E$ is represented by a bounded complex of finite locally free modules of fixed rank, following the proof of the commutativity lemma (proof lines 9553-9556).
Apply the dual statement for finite locally free modules to obtain the signs for $c_i$, $P_i$ and $ch_i$ simultaneously (proof lines 9556-9557).
Alternatively, invoke the splitting principle and observe that dualizing negates the Chern roots, which gives the same conclusion (proof lines 9558-9561).
proof_roadmap: Reduction to a bounded complex of fixed rank (proof lines 9553-9556).
Dual computation for finite locally free modules (proof lines 9556-9557).
Alternative route through Chern roots (proof lines 9558-9561).
difficulty_reason: The lemma computes the effect of dualizing a perfect object on the Chern classes, the components of the Chern character and the power sums, all acquiring the sign $(-1)^i$ (statement lines 9544-9550). Two arguments are recorded: a reduction to bounded complexes of finite locally free modules of fixed rank together with the dual statement in that case, and a splitting-principle route using the negated Chern roots. The reduction and the transport of the sign through the three families of classes are the substance, so the claim is H2.
